opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly, I don't think there's a clean threshold where you can say, "Okay, now we have enough." It's more of a set of signals you look for.

The first thing I ask is not "how much data do we have," but "what kind of data is it?" Most research data that exists in the world is the final product: the polished paper, the clean figure, the theorem that worked. What's missing is the process: the dead ends, the wrong hypotheses, the moment where you look at a plot and say, "Hmm, that's weird," and change direction. If you want a model that can actually *do* research rather than just summarize it, you need data that captures that trajectory. So the first criterion is whether our data has enough of the messy middle, not just the clean ending.

The second signal is diversity of failure modes. If all our logged research trajectories come from one or two people, or one narrow subfield, the model will mostly learn their habits and taste. That can be useful, but it's not general research ability. I want to see that the data covers different kinds of problems, some where the answer comes from a clever experiment, some from a theoretical insight, some from just noticing an anomaly. When adding a new project to the dataset stops surprising us, when the new trajectories start to look structurally similar to ones we already have, that's a hint we've covered a reasonable part of the space.

Third, and this is very practical: can we evaluate it? Before training anything, I want small, well-defined research tasks where we know what good behavior looks like, where we can check whether the model proposed a sensible next experiment or caught a flaw in an argument. If we can't evaluate, then having more data doesn't really help, because we won't know whether training is moving in the right direction.

And then there's a kind of physicist's instinct I bring to it, which is to start small and look for scaling behavior. You don't wait until you think the data is "enough." You train small models on subsets, a quarter of the data, half, all of it, and see whether performance on those research tasks improves smoothly. If you see a clear trend, that tells you the data contains real signal and roughly how much more you'd need. If the curve is flat, then more of the same data probably won't save you, and you need to rethink what you're collecting.

So in short, it's less about a number and more about three questions: does the data capture process rather than just results, is it diverse enough that the model isn't just imitating one person's style, and do small-scale experiments show a trend that's worth betting on? When all three look reasonably positive, that's when I'd feel comfortable starting to train seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says data type matters more than amount and emphasizes research process over polished results, but does not clearly state that many papers can still be low-quality training data.

r002.rationale: The candidate rejects a clean threshold and gives no estimate of roughly ten thousand entries.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses research tasks and model evaluation, but does not frame the model as an interlocutor for debating the team’s ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly my answer is that "enough" is the wrong frame to begin with. People imagine there's some threshold, like a hundred thousand papers or a million experiment logs, and once you cross it you press the button. In my experience it never works like that.

The way I think about it is: what behavior do I want the model to have, and does the data actually contain that behavior? Research isn't just the final paper. The paper is the polished artifact, the part where all the dead ends have been edited out. What makes a researcher good is the process: forming a hypothesis, trying something, seeing it fail, figuring out why it failed, changing direction. If my data is only papers, I have a lot of tokens but almost none of the signal I care about. So the first thing I ask is not "how much" but "does this data contain the reasoning trajectory, including the failures?"

The second thing I look at is diversity rather than volume. In the KAN work, for example, we found that a relatively small number of carefully chosen problems taught us more about what the architecture could and couldn't do than scaling up on one kind of task. A model trained on ten thousand variations of the same problem learns to solve that problem. A model trained on a thousand genuinely different problems starts to learn something closer to a method. So I'd rather have a smaller dataset that spans very different kinds of scientific questions than a huge dataset that's really one question in disguise.

Then there's a practical test I like, which is quite simple: before training anything large, I train something small and look at whether it improves at all on a held-out task that I actually care about. Not a benchmark, a real task, something like "here's an experimental result we haven't published, can you propose a plausible mechanism?" If a small model trained on our data shows even a weak, noisy signal of getting better at that, then I believe scaling will help. If there's no signal at all, more data won't save you. You have the wrong kind of data, not too little of it.

And the last thing, which is maybe more philosophical: I try to be honest about what I'm actually hoping the model will do. If the goal is to automate the parts of research that are already fairly mechanical, like literature search or running parameter sweeps, you need much less than people think, and you could start tomorrow. If the goal is for the model to have genuine scientific taste, to know which question is worth asking, I'm not sure any amount of data gets you there by itself, because taste comes from being in contact with reality and being wrong many times. So my honest answer is: you start when you have data that captures the process, that's diverse, and that shows a signal at small scale. And you stay humble about which part of research you're actually training it to do.

r001.rationale: The response says that many papers may provide lots of tokens but little of the research-process signal it values, so paper volume alone does not ensure useful training data.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that roughly ten thousand collected entries may suffice; it mentions ten thousand variations only as an example of repetitive data.

r003.rationale: It describes testing a model on tasks such as proposing a mechanism, but does not frame the model as an interlocutor for debating the team's ideas.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we want the model to learn. The amount of data alone doesn’t tell you whether it’s enough—you also need to look at its quality, diversity, and relevance to the task.

Then I’d run a small pilot. Train on progressively larger subsets and evaluate on held-out data, making sure there’s no leakage. If training performance improves but validation performance doesn’t, that suggests a generalization problem; we might need more varied data, better labels, or a different modeling approach.

So I’d distinguish having enough data to start from having enough to achieve the final goal. To start, you need a credible experiment and a reliable way to measure progress. Those first experiments help you decide what data to collect next.

r001.rationale: It says quantity alone does not establish sufficiency and emphasizes data quality, but does not distinguish an abundance of research papers from their quality.

r003.rationale: It discusses training and measuring a model, but does not describe the model as an interlocutor for debating the team's ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what we want the model to learn, rather than looking for a particular number of samples. Does the data cover the situations we care about? Is it consistent, and can we set aside a meaningful test set that doesn’t overlap with training?

Then I’d train a small baseline and look at the learning curve. If adding data keeps improving performance on held-out examples, we probably need more. If performance plateaus, I’d investigate whether the limitation is data quality, coverage, or the model itself. You don’t need enough data for the final model to start—you need enough to run an experiment that tells you what to do next.
